lec05kp22-u01-p2-title.text: Robust losses: Huber turns linear beyond c and the ε-insensitive loss ignores errors within ε

lec05kp22-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p2-bridge.text: Squaring lets one outlier dominate least squares. Can the penalty of a large error grow less fast?

lec05kp22-u01-p2-fig1.text: Three losses against the residual e: squared, Huber (c=1) and ε-insensitive (ε=0.5, shaded band costs nothing).

lec05kp22-u01-p2-term:穩健損失.text: **Robust loss**: a loss that is lenient on large errors so that a few bad points no longer dominate.

lec05kp22-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp22-u01-p2-c1.text: **Huber**: $\tfrac12e^2$ for $|e|\le c$ and $c|e|-c^2/2$ beyond; the outlier's influence drops from quadratic to linear.

lec05kp22-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp22-u01-p2-c2.text: **Values**: $e=3$: squared 4.5, Huber ($c=1$) 2.5, ε-insensitive ($\epsilon=0.5$) 2.5; $e=10$: 50, 9.5, 9.5 (they coincide for $|e|>1$ only because of $c=1$, $\epsilon=0.5$).

lec05kp22-u01-p3-title.text: The same 21 points: Huber (c=1) gets slope 2.10, least squares 2.69

lec05kp22-u01-p3-bridge.text: Huber turns large errors linear. On the same 21 points, how far does the outlier bend its line?

lec05kp22-u01-p3-fig1.text: The same 21 points: least squares has slope 2.69 and Huber (c=1) slope 2.10.

lec05kp22-u01-p3-c1.text: **Method** (IRLS, iteratively reweighted least squares): weight 1 when $|e|\le c$ and $c/|e|$ otherwise, repeated until convergence.

lec05kp22-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp22-u01-p3-c2.text: **Result**: Huber ($c=1$) slope 2.099, intercept 0.867; least squares 2.686, $-0.007$; least squares on clean data 2.009, 1.000.

lec05kp22-u01-p3-c3.text: **Three noise draws**: Huber 2.10, 2.14, 2.13; least squares 2.69, 2.95, 2.98. Huber is still slightly off (truth 2) but far less.

lec05kp22-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp22-u01-p4-title.text: SVR: points with error below ε get coefficient 0, so ε is the sparsity knob

lec05kp22-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p4-bridge.text: Huber gives weight 1 when $|e|\le c$ and $c/|e|$ otherwise. If small errors are simply ignored, what does the solution look like?

lec05kp22-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp22-u01-p4-c2.text: **Read from KKT**: error $<\epsilon$ → $\lambda_i=\lambda_i^{\star}=0$; support vectors = points with error $\ge\epsilon$; error $>\epsilon$ → $\lambda=C$.

lec05kp22-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp22-u01-p5-title.text: A larger ε keeps fewer support vectors: 58 at ε=0.01, 5 at ε=0.5, but the error rises from 0.0008 to 0.055

lec05kp22-u01-p5-bridge.text: $\epsilon$ is the sparsity knob. As it is turned, how do the support-vector count and the accuracy change?

lec05kp22-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp22-eps

lec05kp22-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp22-u01-p5-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): $y=\sin x+$ noise (sd 0.15), 60 points, Gaussian kernel $\gamma=0.5$, $C=10$.

lec05kp22-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp22-u01-p5-c3.text: **Mean squared error against the true sin**: 0.0008, 0.0020, 0.0038, 0.0175, 0.0551, 0.3455. A larger $\epsilon$ gives a sparser but coarser fit.

lec05kp22-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp22-u01-p6-title.text: Ridge regression: set ε to 0 and use equalities to get the closed form g(x)=yᵀ(K+C·I)⁻¹p

lec05kp22-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p6-bridge.text: A larger ε gives a sparser but coarser fit; what if ε is turned to 0?

lec05kp22-u01-p6-term:脊迴歸.name: term:Ridge regression
lec05kp22-u01-p6-term:脊迴歸.text: **Ridge regression**: least squares with a penalty on the norm, done in the RKHS.

lec05kp22-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp22-u01-p6-c1.text: **Method**: set $\epsilon=0$, $w_0=0$ and use equalities: minimize $\mathcal C\|w\|^2+\sum\xi_i^2$ with $\mathcal C=\tfrac1{2C}$ (a larger $\mathcal C$ squeezes harder).

lec05kp22-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp22-u01-p6-c2.text: **Closed form**: $g(x)=y^T(\mathcal K+\mathcal CI)^{-1}p$; it differs from the kernel least squares of KP21 only by $\mathcal CI$.

lec05kp22-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp22-u01-p6-c3.text: **The price**: with squared error and equality constraints no point is a free zero-error point, so sparsity is lost; no free lunch.

lec05kp22-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp22-u01-p7-title.text: Ridge steadies almost collinear features: from 0 to 0.1 the coefficients go from −170 and 171 to 0.49 and 0.49

lec05kp22-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p7-bridge.text: Ridge regression differs from kernel least squares only by $\mathcal CI$. With a linear kernel, what does this term buy?

lec05kp22-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp22-u01-p7-c1.text: **Two forms** (linear kernel): $w=(X^TX+\mathcal CI)^{-1}X^Ty=X^T(XX^T+\mathcal CI)^{-1}y$; with 15 points, 4 features and $\mathcal C=0.8$ the largest gap is $6\times10^{-16}$.

lec05kp22-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp22-u01-p7-c2.text: **Collinear example** (designed here): two nearly identical columns (differing by $10^{-4}$): $\mathcal C=0$: $w=(-170.0,171.0)$, condition number $5\times10^8$; $\mathcal C=0.1$: $(0.49,0.49)$, condition number 776.

lec05kp22-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp22-u01-p7-c3.text: **Meaning**: adding a small positive number on the diagonal is a standard numerical stabilizer; the price is coefficients pulled toward 0.

lec05kp22-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp22-u01-p8-title.text: On the same outlier data: Huber 2.10 and ε-insensitive 2.12 resist it, ridge 2.68 does not

lec05kp22-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p8-bridge.text: Ridge regression steadies almost collinear features with $\mathcal CI$. Does it also resist that outlier? Put four methods on the same data.

lec05kp22-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp22-u01-p8-c1.text: **Slopes** (truth 2): least squares 2.686; Huber ($c=1$) 2.099; ε-insensitive ($\epsilon=0.5$, $C=10$) 2.122; ridge ($\mathcal C=0.1$) 2.679.

lec05kp22-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp22-u01-p8-c2.text: **Nonzero coefficients**: ε-insensitive has only 4 support vectors out of 21 points; the other three use all 21.

lec05kp22-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp22-u01-p8-c3.text: **To remember**: Huber = large errors linear; ε-insensitive = small errors ignored (sparse); ridge = $\epsilon=0$ for a closed form (not sparse). Ridge resists collinearity, not outliers (one dataset, one outlier).

lec05kp22-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp22-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: the Huber threshold c is a knob, with slope 2.045 at c=0.2 and back to least squares at c=20

lec05kp22-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p9-bridge.text: Huber resists the outlier and ridge does not. What value of the Huber threshold $c$ makes an error large?

lec05kp22-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp22-u01-p9-c2.text: **Meaning**: a large $c$ puts every error in the quadratic zone, which is least squares; a small $c$ nearly ignores the outlier.

lec05kp22-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp22-u01-p9-c3.text: **Trade-off**: choose $c$ to match the noise level (sd 0.3 here); least squares on clean data gives 2.009.

lec05kp22-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp22-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, what each loss charges

lec05kp22-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p10-bridge.text: The Huber threshold decides which errors are large. Back to the definitions: by hand, what do two errors cost under the Huber and the ε-insensitive loss?

lec05kp22-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp22-u01-p10-q1.text: **Setup**: residual $e=y-g(x)$; Huber with $c=1$ and ε-insensitive with $\epsilon=0.5$.

lec05kp22-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp22-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 1**: what is the Huber loss at $e=0.5$ and at $e=3$?

lec05kp22-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp22-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: what is the ε-insensitive loss at $e=0.3$ and at $e=2$?

lec05kp22-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp22-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp22-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp22-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked for the Huber loss at $e=0.5,3$ and the ε-insensitive loss at $e=0.3,2$. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp22-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp22-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: a small error costs the same under Huber and squared (0.125) but 0 under ε-insensitive; a large error grows linearly under both robust losses.

steps.label: Robust and ridge regression
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. Least squares fearing outliers, the three robust losses, the KKT reading and sparsity of epsilon-insensitive regression, the closed form and the two forms of ridge regression and the 'to remember' line follow the source; every number (slope 2.009 becoming 2.686, Huber 2.099, 58 down to 2 support vectors in the epsilon sweep, the primal-dual gap 6e-16, the collinear -170 and 171, the four-method comparison, the c sweep, the practice 0.125, 2.5, 0 and 1.5) was recomputed by a program and these experiments were designed for this lecture (added); the pages state honestly that Huber is still slightly off, that a larger epsilon gives sparser but coarser fits and that ridge regression itself does not resist outliers. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: The outlier
steps.speakerNotes: The kernel least squares of KP21 minimizes the squared error. This page asks what happens when one point is badly wrong. First the outlier: a point far from the trend of the others, an extreme value or a wrong label, with a larger effect at the edge of the x range. The setup was designed here: 20 points y equal to 2x plus 1 plus noise with standard deviation 0.3, x from 0 to 4, plus one outlier at x equal to 5 with y raised by 10. The result: the least-squares slope goes from 2.009 to 2.686 and the intercept from 1.000 to minus 0.007, where the truth is 2 and 1; three noise draws give 2.69, 2.95 and 2.98. Why: squaring makes a large error's contribution grow quadratically, so it dominates the solution. The next page asks whether the penalty can grow less fast.

steps.label: Robust losses
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said squaring lets one outlier dominate least squares. This page asks whether the penalty of a large error can grow less fast. First the robust loss: a loss that is lenient on large errors so that a few bad points no longer dominate. Then the epsilon-insensitive loss: the larger of |e| minus epsilon and 0, so errors within epsilon cost nothing. Huber: one half e squared for |e| at most c and c times |e| minus half of c squared beyond; the outlier's influence drops from quadratic to linear. Values: e equal to 3: squared 4.5, Huber with c equal to 1 gives 2.5, epsilon-insensitive with epsilon 0.5 gives 2.5; e equal to 10: 50, 9.5 and 9.5. The next page fits the same data with Huber.

steps.label: Huber fit
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said Huber turns large errors linear. This page asks how far the outlier bends the line on the same 21 points. The method is IRLS, iteratively reweighted least squares: weight 1 when |e| is at most c and c over |e| otherwise, repeated until convergence. The result: Huber with c equal to 1 has slope 2.099 and intercept 0.867; least squares has 2.686 and minus 0.007; least squares on clean data has 2.009 and 1.000. Three noise draws: Huber 2.10, 2.14 and 2.13; least squares 2.69, 2.95 and 2.98. Huber is still slightly off, the truth being 2, but far less. The next page asks what the solution looks like if small errors are ignored instead.

steps.label: ε-insensitive regression
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said Huber gives weight 1 when |e| is at most c and c over |e| otherwise. This page asks what the solution looks like if small errors are simply ignored. The objective: half the squared norm of w plus C times the sum of the slack variables, with errors within epsilon plus slack; the regressor is the sum over the support vectors of lambda star minus lambda times K, plus w0. Read from KKT: points with error below epsilon have lambda and lambda star equal to 0; support vectors are points with error at least epsilon; points with error above epsilon have lambda at the upper bound C. The meaning is that epsilon is the sparsity knob, and epsilon equal to 0 with y equal to plus or minus 1 gives back the classification SVM. The next page turns epsilon.

steps.label: Turning ε
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said epsilon is the sparsity knob. This page asks how the support-vector count and the accuracy change as it is turned. The setup was designed here: y equal to sin x plus noise with standard deviation 0.15, 60 points, Gaussian kernel gamma 0.5 and C equal to 10. Support vectors: epsilon of 0.01 gives 58; 0.1 gives 29; 0.2 gives 9; 0.3 gives 6; 0.5 gives 5; 1.0 gives 2. Mean squared error against the true sin: 0.0008, 0.0020, 0.0038, 0.0175, 0.0551 and 0.3455. A larger epsilon gives a sparser but coarser fit. The next page asks what happens when epsilon is turned to 0.

steps.label: Ridge regression
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said a larger epsilon gives a sparser but coarser fit. This page asks what happens when epsilon is turned to 0. First ridge regression: least squares with a penalty on the norm, done in the RKHS. The method: set epsilon to 0 and w0 to 0 and use equalities, minimizing script C times the squared norm of w plus the sum of squared slacks, with script C equal to one over 2C. The closed form: g of x is y transpose times the inverse of K plus script C I times p; it differs from the kernel least squares of KP21 only by script C I. The price: with epsilon equal to 0 no point is a free zero-error point, so sparsity is lost; there is no free lunch. The next page looks at what this term buys with a linear kernel.

steps.label: Collinearity
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said ridge regression differs from kernel least squares only by script C I. This page asks what this term buys with a linear kernel. The two forms: w is the inverse of X transpose X plus script C I times X transpose y, which also equals X transpose times the inverse of X X transpose plus script C I times y; with 15 points, 4 features and script C equal to 0.8 the largest gap is 6 times 10 to the minus 16. The collinear example was designed here: two nearly identical columns differing by 10 to the minus 4: with script C equal to 0, w is (minus 170.0, 171.0) with condition number 5 times 10 to the 8; with script C equal to 0.1 it is (0.49, 0.49) with condition number 776. The meaning is that adding a small positive number on the diagonal is a standard numerical stabilizer; the price is coefficients pulled toward 0. The next page puts four methods on the same data.

steps.label: Four methods compared
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said ridge regression steadies with script C I. This page asks whether it also resists that outlier, putting four methods on the same data. Slopes, the truth being 2: least squares 2.686; Huber with c equal to 1 gives 2.099; epsilon-insensitive with epsilon 0.5 and C equal to 10 gives 2.122; ridge with script C equal to 0.1 gives 2.679. Nonzero coefficients: epsilon-insensitive has only 4 support vectors out of 21 points; the other three use all 21. To remember: Huber makes large errors linear; epsilon-insensitive ignores small errors and is sparse; ridge uses epsilon equal to 0 for a closed form and loses sparsity. Ridge resists collinearity, not outliers. The next extension page looks at the Huber threshold c.

steps.label: Extension: threshold c
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said Huber resists the outlier and ridge does not. This extension asks what value of the Huber threshold c makes an error large. Sweeping c on the same 21 points: c of 0.2 gives 2.045; 0.5 gives 2.054; 1 gives 2.099; 2 gives 2.188; 5 gives 2.455; 20 gives 2.686. The meaning is that a large c puts every error in the quadratic zone, which is least squares, while a small c nearly ignores the outlier. The trade-off: choose c to match the noise level, standard deviation 0.3 here; least squares on clean data gives 2.009. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the Huber threshold decides which errors are large. This page poses an exercise back on the definitions: the residual e is y minus g of x; Huber with c equal to 1 and epsilon-insensitive with epsilon equal to 0.5. Question 1: what is the Huber loss at e equal to 0.5 and at e equal to 3? Question 2: what is the epsilon-insensitive loss at e equal to 0.3 and at e equal to 2? Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: e equal to 0.5 is within 1: half times 0.25, which is 0.125; e equal to 3 is beyond 1: 1 times 3 minus a half, which is 2.5. The squared loss would give 0.125 and 4.5. Question 2: e equal to 0.3: the larger of 0.3 minus 0.5 and 0, which is 0; e equal to 2: the larger of 2 minus 0.5 and 0, which is 1.5. Check: a small error costs the same under Huber and squared but 0 under epsilon-insensitive; a large error grows linearly under both robust losses. That finishes robust regression and ridge regression; the next knowledge point looks at decision trees.
